S1-Q3c.hook: O2 rides on haemoglobin in red cells; CO2 mostly travels in plasma as hydrogencarbonate

S1-Q3c.q: What is the main way oxygen is carried in the blood?
S1-Q3c.right: As oxyhaemoglobin in red blood cells
S1-Q3c.why: Oxygen binds to haemoglobin in red cells to form oxyhaemoglobin; very little dissolves in plasma.
S1-Q3c.hint: Which iron-containing pigment picks up this gas, and in which cells is it found?
S1-Q3c.hook: Haemoglobin is an oxygen taxi: picks up at the lungs, drops off at the tissues

S1-Q3c.q: What goes in the table for arterial and venous pulmonary blood? (2 points)
S1-Q3c.right: Arterial: CO2 high, O2 low; venous: CO2 low, O2 high
wrong: Arterial: CO2 low, O2 high; venous: CO2 high, O2 low
Arterial: CO2 high, O2 high; venous: CO2 low, O2 low
Arterial: CO2 high, O2 low; venous: CO2 high, O2 low
S1-Q3c.why: Two points: pulmonary artery blood, going to the lungs, is high in CO2 and low in O2; pulmonary vein blood, coming back, is the reverse.
S1-Q3c.hint: Pulmonary artery blood is heading to the lungs; pulmonary vein blood is coming back. What changed?
S1-Q3c.board: Are CO2 and O2 levels high or low in pulmonary arterial blood and in pulmonary venous blood? (2 points)
S1-Q3c.hook: Pulmonary vessels flip the rule: the artery carries 'used' blood, the vein carries fresh
keys: high in CO2 and low in O2

S1-Q5d.q: What are the two common blood grouping systems?
S1-Q5d.why: The ABO system (A, B, AB, O) and the Rhesus system (positive or negative) are the two main ones.
S1-Q5d.hint: Think of the letters on a blood bag, then the plus or minus sign after them.
S1-Q5d.hook: Your blood group has two parts, like 'A positive': A is the ABO part, positive is Rhesus

S1-Q5d.q: Why is it important to know a person's blood group?
wrong: To work out their heart rate
To choose which antibiotic to give
To find out if they are anaemic
S1-Q5d.why: Wrong-group blood makes the recipient's antibodies clump the donor red cells, which can be fatal.
S1-Q5d.hint: Think about giving blood to a patient, and a mother whose baby's blood differs from hers.
S1-Q5d.hook: Wrong blood = clumped blood: the recipient's antibodies attack the donor's red cells
keys: antibodies clump the donor red cells

S2-Q5a.q: On the diagram, which vessel is B?
S2-Q5a.why: B is the pulmonary artery, taking blood to the lungs; A is the aorta, taking blood to the body.
S2-Q5a.hint: Follow each from its ventricle: one arches over to the body, the other heads to the lungs.
S2-Q5a.hook: Right to the lungs, left to the rest: pulmonary artery from the right, aorta from the left

S2-Q5a.q: What happens to the labelled valve when the ventricles contract?
S2-Q5a.why: Blood forced out of the ventricle pushes the semilunar valve open; it shuts when the ventricle relaxes.
S2-Q5a.hint: Blood is being forced out of the ventricle into the artery. What must the valve do to let it?
S2-Q5a.board: What happens to a semilunar valve when the ventricles contract?
S2-Q5a.hook: Valves are one-way doors: blood pushing forward opens them, blood falling back slams them

S2-Q5a.q: Where should X (the pacemaker) go on the diagram?
S2-Q5a.right: In the wall of the right atrium
wrong: In the wall of the left atrium
In the septum between the ventricles
At the base of the aorta
S2-Q5a.why: The pacemaker (SA node) is in the upper wall of the right atrium, near where the vena cava enters.
S2-Q5a.hint: Which upper chamber does blood from the body flow into first? Look in its wall.
S2-Q5a.board: Where in the heart is the pacemaker located?
S2-Q5a.hook: SA node: Sits At the right atrium, the heart's built-in pacemaker

S2-Q5a.q: How does plasma CO2 change between A and B, and why? (2 points)
S2-Q5a.right: Higher in B: respiring cells added CO2; A lost CO2 in the lungs
wrong: Higher in A: respiring cells added CO2; B lost CO2 in the lungs
Higher in B: it took in CO2 from the air in the lungs
The same in both: CO2 stays in the red cells all the way
S2-Q5a.why: Two points: CO2 is higher in B (pulmonary artery), as respiring body cells added it; A (aorta) carries blood that lost CO2 in the lungs.
S2-Q5a.hint: Where has the blood in each vessel just been: the body tissues or the lungs?
S2-Q5a.hook: Aorta: fresh from the lungs. Pulmonary artery: back from the body, loaded with CO2

S2-Q5a.q: Which is a structural difference between an artery and a vein?
S2-Q5a.right: Veins have valves; arteries do not
wrong: Arteries have valves; veins do not
Veins have thicker walls than arteries
S2-Q5a.why: Blood in veins is at low pressure, so valves stop it flowing backwards; arteries have thick walls instead.
S2-Q5a.hint: Arteries carry blood at high pressure, veins at low. How would wall, lumen or backflow differ?
S2-Q5a.hook: Veins are low-pressure lanes: thin walls, wide lumen, and valves like one-way doors

S2-Q5b.q: What are the two circuits called?
S2-Q5b.why: The pulmonary circuit takes blood to the lungs; the systemic circuit takes it round the rest of the body.
S2-Q5b.hint: Blood leaves the heart on two loops: one only to the lungs, one round the rest of the body.
S2-Q5b.board: What are the two circuits of the human circulatory system called?
S2-Q5b.hook: A figure of eight: one loop through the lungs (pulmonary), one round the body (systemic)

S2-Q5b.q: Describe the pathway of blood in the pulmonary circuit.
S2-Q5b.right: Right ventricle, pulmonary artery, lungs, pulmonary vein, left atrium
wrong: Right ventricle, pulmonary vein, lungs, pulmonary artery, left atrium
Left ventricle, pulmonary artery, lungs, pulmonary vein, right atrium
Right atrium, pulmonary artery, lungs, pulmonary vein, left ventricle
S2-Q5b.why: Name the circuit and its structures in order: right ventricle, pulmonary artery, lungs, pulmonary vein, left atrium.
S2-Q5b.hint: Pick a loop and start at the ventricle that pumps into it. Then which artery, organ, vein, chamber?
S2-Q5b.hook: Starts on the Right, ends on the Left: out by the pulmonary artery, home by the vein

S2-Q5b.q: What could happen to the heart if a coronary artery were fully blocked? (2 points)
S2-Q5b.right: Heart muscle gets no oxygen and dies
wrong: Heart muscle gets extra oxygen and grows
The heart beats faster and more strongly
Blood bypasses the lungs and the heart rests
S2-Q5b.why: Two of: the muscle it supplies gets no blood or oxygen, so those cells can't respire and die, which is a heart attack.
S2-Q5b.hint: What does this artery normally bring to heart muscle? What happens to cells cut off from it?
S2-Q5b.hook: A blocked coronary is a cut fuel line: no oxygen, so that muscle stops respiring and dies

S2-Q5b.right: Force of blood on the vessel walls
wrong: Speed of blood through the veins
Amount of blood in the body
S2-Q5b.why: Blood pressure is the push of blood on artery walls; beats per minute is the heart (or pulse) rate.
S2-Q5b.hint: As the heart pumps, what does the blood push against inside each artery?
S2-Q5b.hook: Blood pressure is like water pressure in a hose: the push on the walls, not the speed
keys: push of blood on artery walls

S2-Q5c.q: On the graph, what causes each steep rise in pressure?
S2-Q5c.why: Each steep rise is the left ventricle contracting and forcing blood into the arteries: put X there.
S2-Q5c.hint: When the ventricle squeezes, arterial pressure shoots up. Find the steepest climb on the graph.
S2-Q5c.board: What causes each steep rise in arterial blood pressure during a heartbeat?
S2-Q5c.hook: Each spike on the trace is a ventricle squeeze: systole sends the pressure shooting up

S2-Q5c.q: From the graph, work out the heart rate, showing your working. (2 points)
S2-Q5c.right: One beat takes 0.5 s, so 60 / 0.5 = 120 bpm
wrong: One beat takes 0.5 s, so 60 x 0.5 = 30 bpm
One beat takes 1 s, so 60 / 1 = 60 bpm
One beat takes 0.25 s, so 60 / 0.25 = 240 bpm
S2-Q5c.why: Two points: one beat (peak to peak) takes 0.5 s, then divide 60 seconds by it: 60 / 0.5 = 120 beats per minute.
S2-Q5c.hint: Find the time from one peak to the next. How many of those fit into 60 seconds?
S2-Q5c.board: A graph shows one heartbeat every 0.5 s. Work out the heart rate in bpm. (2 points)
S2-Q5c.hook: Beats per minute = 60 divided by the seconds per beat: half a second each gives 120

S2-Q5c.right: No: 120 bpm is too high for rest
wrong: Yes: 120 bpm is a normal resting rate
Yes: athletes always have fast hearts
No: athletes rest at over 150 bpm
S2-Q5c.why: A resting rate is about 60-80 bpm (lower in a fit athlete), so 120 bpm means the athlete is exercising.
S2-Q5c.hint: Compare your answer to (ii) with a typical resting heart rate. Is it higher or lower?
S2-Q5c.board: An athlete's heart rate is 120 bpm. Is the athlete at rest?
S2-Q5c.hook: A resting heart ticks over at about 70: 120 is a jogging heart, not a resting one

S2-Q5d.q: Why do cardiac muscle cells have so many mitochondria? (2 points)
S2-Q5d.right: Heart never rests so needs lots of ATP, made by aerobic respiration
wrong: Heart never rests so needs lots of ATP, made by anaerobic respiration
Heart rests between beats so needs little ATP from respiration
Heart needs a big oxygen store, which mitochondria hold for it
S2-Q5d.why: Two points: heart muscle contracts nonstop and needs lots of energy (ATP); mitochondria release it by aerobic respiration, so it does not tire.
S2-Q5d.hint: How often does heart muscle rest? What do mitochondria make, and by which type of respiration?
S2-Q5d.hook: A heart that never rests needs a power station on every corner: mitochondria everywhere
